content_html:
Mouse droppings are usually small, dark, and elongated, often with tapered ends, but appearance alone does not confirm species or age. Location, gnaw marks, nesting material, and fresh deposits add context. Do not dry-sweep or vacuum rodent droppings because that can aerosolize contaminated dust.

Look at size, shape, and distribution

Mouse droppings are generally much smaller than rat droppings and often appear along travel routes, in drawers, pantries, or behind appliances. Photographing them beside a ruler helps comparison without handling them.

Look for supporting signs in the same area

Small gnaw marks, damaged packages, tracks in dust, and nesting material support the identification. One dark particle could be insect material or debris and is not enough to confirm mice.

Do not judge freshness by touching droppings

Color and sheen vary with humidity, diet, and time, so handling droppings to judge age is not worthwhile. Clean them safely and then monitor for new deposits.

Wet and disinfect before removal

Ventilate an enclosed area when appropriate, wear gloves, and apply an appropriate disinfectant according to its label before wiping material up. Do not dry-sweep or vacuum; extensive activity or inaccessible nesting may justify professional pest control.
